extracted.intended_audience: improv performers, improv students, and workshop participants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing short-form long-form improv scenes by prioritizing honesty, truthful offers, and collaborative listening (exercises like 'Park Bench of Truth'). Focus is on generating comedy from real, mundane details rather than overt jokiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play honestly (not jokey)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book tells you to not be jokey. It tells you to play your scenes realistically with honesty, bravery and integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to be funny as your primary goal; instead play the scene realistically. The post emphasizes that honest, realistic play will frequently produce hilarious ideas without deliberate joke-making. The author admits often failing to live up to this standard, underscoring its centrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal truth (Park Bench of Truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Play close to yourself: have an honest conversation with your scene partner under fictional but not very theatrical circumstances (the 'Park Bench of Truth' exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin this exercise by stating an honest opinion you hold rather than inventing a fictional premise. The post includes full scene transcripts showing how everyday admissions (e.g., 'I eat sweet potato fries every day') produce multiple comedic moments organically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen really hard and support your scene partner
rubrics_metrics.description: All you need to do is be brave, be yourself, listen really hard and support your scene partner’s ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to what your partner offers and build on it. Doing what your partner wants makes collaboration easier than trying to impose your own comic intent. Examples: follow a partner's implicit comedic choices rather than correcting or explaining them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brave — embrace the fear of being truthful onstage
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to be brave, because it is very scary to get in front of an audience, tell them you are going to be funny and then just be honest instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that honesty may feel vulnerable; commit to it anyway. The post frames bravery as necessary because being yourself onstage can feel risky but is a source of strong comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid telegraphing jokes; keep the audience off-guard
rubrics_metrics.description: If you start a scene by telegraphing that you think you’re a hoot and that this is about to be very funny, a certain percentage of them... are going to lean back into a 'Prove It' stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start scenes sincerely so the audience doesn't expect jokes; surprise creates bigger laughs. The post contrasts beginning jokey vs. beginning sincere and notes that sincere openings let you 'surprise' the audience for bigger payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor nonsense with truthful elements
rubrics_metrics.description: You need big truthful elements to be placed next to the nonsense or no one is going to buy into the nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because improv lacks special effects/real props, believable relationships, reactions and truthful details make ridiculous premises believable. The Marvel movie analogy illustrates how truthful elements let audiences suspend disbelief for absurd premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start scenes boring to create contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: See 'Start Your Improv Scene Boring' — the idea that beginning with a mundane, truthful scene can make ensuing comedy land better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using boring/realistic beginnings provides a foundation from which comedic heightening or absurd turns feel earned. The post refers readers to another page with multiple examples of this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer specific, mundane details as comedic offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Small, concrete truthful details (air fryer stories, popcorn, sweet potato fries) often create many funny moments without intentional joke-writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity is fertile: personal anecdotes and concrete habits become comedic seeds. The post's scene transcripts highlight multiple funny beats that arise simply from mundane specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start scenes with an honest opinion to generate options
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing honest opinions (e.g., 'I wish summer would never end') gives immediate opportunities for comedic exploration and alternate choices between partners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An honest opening yields many divergent but usable comedic directions; pick the option that best serves the scene and partner. The Duane/Jennifer example shows how differing but sincere opinions create multiple funny pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize collaborative comedy over being 'right' or educational
rubrics_metrics.description: We aren’t trying to educate our scene partners or the general public when we do improv. We are trying to collaboratively build comedy scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't derail a scene to prove you're right. If a partner's choice bothers you, stop working with them outside the scene — but onstage, work with their offers to build comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: If your partner finds something funny, go with it
rubrics_metrics.description: If your scene partner thinks it is funny that your character thinks X, then go with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when you personally disagree, accept the partner's read — it's easier and more effective to support their comic choices than to resist. The post emphasizes doing what the partner wants to do if you can tell what that is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t take scene choices personally; separate character from self
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not offensive to make a scene where a comedic character shares the same point of view you do — this is about creating a comedy scene, not mocking you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember the distinction between performer and character. If someone's humor consistently offends you in practice, avoid working with them; but onstage, treat exaggerated or different character beliefs as offers for comedy rather than personal attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover comedic material first; frame, heighten and leverage later
rubrics_metrics.description: Funny ideas that naturally emerge from truthful play are powerful; framing, heightening and leveraging those ideas is a subsequent step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus first on discovering organic comedic moments through truth and listening; shaping and escalating those moments can come later (the author defers detailed techniques for framing/heightening to another post).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer realistic offers over theatrical set-ups in this exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: For Park Bench of Truth you don't need to invent elaborate fictional circumstances; playing an honest conversation in a plausible situation is sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overly theatrical premises for this exercise; the power comes from plausible, low-theatricality contexts that reveal truthful behavior and create comedic opportunities.
